articles.title: DM My Rep! The Top Lawyers, Managers and Agents Driving the Creator Economy
articles.author: Kimberly Nordyke

paras.en: This is their world and, for better or worse, we’re just living in it. Those populating the creator economy are swaying elections (Hasan Piker), reimagining independent film (Mark Fischbach, aka Markiplier) and selling out capsule collections at the Gap (seriously, Hailey Bieber, are there any of those jeans left?). But even the best business and marketing minds on the internet can’t build an empire without a team.

Without their reps, the world these creators built would be a fraction of what it is today … and, worst of all, we’d have no idea who to call daddy. So let’s take a look at the most powerful reps in the creator space, all they made happen and all the money they moved in 2026.
Ali Berman, Raina Penchansky, Oren Rosenbaum and Hilary Williams

UTA Creators and its in-house Digital Brand Architects are home to a daunting roster that includes Markiplier, Kareem Rahma, Colin and Samir and Olandria Carthen. Among the year’s marquee moves were populating Netflix’s new video podcast slate (The Rotten Files With Stephanie Soo), brokering that infamous MrBeast-James Patterson novel collab, expanding Emma Chamberlain’s Chamberlain Coffee (hello, Abbot Kinney!) and putting Alix Earle with the Netflix series Earle Meets World.
Keith Bielory, Melissa DeMarco and Jade Sherman

Gersh’s digital division sees Sherman, Bielory and DeMarco continuing to push clients further into mainstream entertainment and culture, facilitating record-breaking runs for Broadway’s Chicago thanks to reality star clients Ariana Madix, Whitney Leavitt and Mark Ballas. The team also helped online health expert Doctor Mike surpass 30 million followers and snagged Eli Rallo a deal for a book that became a New York Times best-seller.
Payton Booker, Skye Petrie and Alexis Ramos

Ramos has grown Sixteenth’s sports division from the ground up, now representing top sports names in the NFL, WNBA and track and field. Petrie brought a massive U.K. roster to the company, helping British internet stars like Maddie Borge go global. Booker has secured major partnerships, including a $90,000 brand campaign for Charles Brockman III and an $80,000 Tinder partnership for The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Layla Taylor.

Founding Palette during the 2020 TikTok boom, Daks and DeAngelis have since built out a roster of talent spanning comedy, lifestyle and infotainment including Spanish news creator Carlos Eduardo Espina (he launched his Creator Cup, which twice sold out MLS’ Houston Dynamo stadium) and Roblox star Lana Rae. The latter’s consumer product line has done more than $20 million at retail in the past five months.

Managing partners Brian Sokolik and Nate Ruff recruited Das to the management company where he’s since made a name for himself for representing social impact creators. For client Hunter Prosper, a storyteller and interviewer, he closed a book deal and helped him launch a series with Barack Obama’s production company Higher Ground. Das also helped video creator Jesus Morales, who tells Latinx stories around Los Angeles, launch a nonprofit that has already earned six figures in donations.

Davis closed a reported $100 million first-of-its-kind pact for Jay Shetty and his On Purpose podcast to have joint exclusive rights at Netflix and Spotify. Dayeh and Davis also helped reality stars Paige DeSorbo and Hannah Berner secure major brand partnerships, including Hannah’s multiyear ambassadorship with Lululemon.

As Entertainment 360 seeks a bigger piece of the digital pie, Devlin joined this year to further expand its creator business. This year, she brokered Paige DeSorbo’s Super Bowl commercial with Kinder Bueno and negotiated finance guru Vivian Tu’s second book, which quickly became a New York Times best-seller.
Matt Dysart and Eric Perlmutter-Gumbiner

Serving as corporate and strategic adviser to digital marketing and talent firms, Perlmutter-Gumbiner works with creator-led Palette Media Talent Management and Marketing, Jake Rosen Entertainment, Get Engaged Media, Underscore Talent Agency, Made by All and Dhar Mann Studios. Dysart is heavily invested in the digital space, representing Slow Ventures, Kynetic Content, UnderCurrent, Palette Media and Creator Society, among others.

Parker Management kicked off the year by acquiring Estate Five, expanding their portfolio of creators across the fashion and beauty spaces. Recent signings include Alex Bennett, Greg Navage, Abigail Erb and Michelle Riley, joining a deep bench of top lifestyle, family and home creators, as well as Bachelor Nation talent. The firm secured campaigns with Google Pixel, Abercrombie & Fitch, Tuckernuck and Lincoln, to name a few.
Lisa Filipelli, Brittany Maxwell and Caroline Nardilla

Select keeps leaning into the intersection of the creator economy and Hollywood, delivering new seasons of The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives (not messy work at all!) and franchise expansion TSLOMW: Orange County, both populated with Select clients. They also launched Select Sports, which reimagines athlete representation for the social media era, landing Super Bowl campaigns with Meta x Oakley glasses and Toyota for Sky Brown and Oksana Masters.
Dylan Flinn, Mallory Llewellyn and Kyle Stevens

Llewellyn landed four of her clients on Netflix’s Calabasas Confidential, for which she serves as consulting producer. Stevens helped Kareem Rahma turn SubwayTakes into an Emmy-nominated series, while launching Rahma’s second show, Keep the Meter Running. Flinn has become the go-to manager for top AI creators, landing one of the first celebrity likeness deals with HiggsfieldAI and securing a studio development deal for AI content creator Chloe vs History. Team History!
Arleta Fowler, Andrew Graham, Brent Weinstein and Sophie Wiener

Over the past year, the agency has signed some of the biggest creators in the world, including Rhett + Link, Valkyrae, Stokes Twins, Deestroying, Rebecca Zamolo, Nara Smith, Jack Goldburg (aka Jack’s Dining Room), Reckless Ben, Max “Career Ladder” Klymenko and Reece Feldman. In June, CAA and Integrated Media Co. launched a $250 million venture called Compound Creative Holdings, aimed at acquiring, operating and growing companies in the creator economy.

Freytag and Ginsberg have spent nearly a decade building careers and brokering livestreaming’s biggest deals. Loaded represents the largest share of Twitch livestreamers by watch time, including TheBurntPeanut, Cinna, Maya Higa and Shroud. They’ve landed recent deals with Google, EA, Epic Games and Tencent and recently negotiated a “Protect the Peanut” campaign with Battlefield, one of EA’s most successful creator campaigns.
Joe Gilliland, Josh Morgan and Marcela Woessner

Woessner inked gymnast and Instagram star Livvy Dunne’s partnership with Miller Lite and turned an embarrassing viral moment (sweat stains are unavoidable!) into a partnership with deodorant brand Secret. The Team acquired Provisions, a leading golf creator agency founded by Gilliland and Morgan. The two developed the Creator Classic, a tournament where 12 of YouTube’s top golf creators compete, and built Your Golf Tour, a YouTube series featuring the sport’s biggest creators and pros.
Ryan Goodell, Todd Rubenstein and Kevin Yorn

Alix Earle has evolved from creator to entrepreneur under Yorn and Rubenstein, who helped launch her skin care brand, Reale Actives, and negotiated the Netflix series Earle Meets World. Yorn advised Hailey Bieber on her 2026 Gap collection (long live the baggy jeans renaissance), among many major brand deals, while Rubenstein represented the multitalented Charli D’Amelio (see page 48). As for Goodell, he has chef Nick DiGiovanni (75 million-plus followers), who served as Fox Sports’ official chef for the FIFA World Cup this year.

Night has had another blockbuster year, acquiring IRL marketing firm Experiential Supply Co. Nelson brokered deals for Twitch star Kai Cenat’s record-breaking Streamer University with partners including Red Bull, Dell and Fortnite. Jacobs helped the true-crime show Morbid sell out Radio City Music Hall on a live tour. He also launched Unbiased Politics, a daily video show with lawyer influencer Jordan Berman. Jacobson closed deals for beauty vlogger Bretman Rock (19 million on Instagram) to front a global campaign for Kate Spade New York and a partnership to make him the face of K-beauty brand Dr. Groot in the U.S. Rosen’s client Noah Beck has been showcasing his acting talent in the popular Tubi rom-com franchise Sideline: The QB and Me, with Rosen ironing out deals for the second and upcoming third and final film, along with helping get him cast on Fox’s Baywatch reboot.

Outshine Talent has built out its sports business significantly, representing internet-famous baseball stars like the Savannah Bananas’ Kyle “KJ” Jackson and RobertAnthony Cruz (aka Coach RAC), who just launched a custom product line with Under Armour. Adam Kaller, Ryan Pastorek and Lauren Partipilo Schwartz

In a landmark creator economy story, Mark Fischbach (aka Markiplier) pushed fans to call theaters to screen his self-funded $3 million Iron Lung. In addition, Pastorek and Partipilo sealed Hannah Berner and Paige DeSorbo’s Giggly Squad signing of a multiyear deal with SiriusXM. Partipilo also negotiated for RHOSLC‘s Bronwyn Newport to appear on this upcoming season of The Traitors.

paras.en: Founded by former Morning Brew executives, Smooth Media has built one of the fastest-growing management firms representing knowledge creators. It partnered with Colin and Samir to build creator industry publication The Publish Press, and, just this month, creator Cat Goetze (known online as CatGPT) took an equity stake in the company and joined as a strategic adviser.

McNeily recently closed a podcast deal for top horror creator Heidi Wong and put scripted adaptations of lifestyle influencer Tinx’s best-selling books The Shift and Hotter in the Hamptons into development at Amazon and Hulu. Worthy Patterson, Mariam Rastegar Ross and Eman Redwan

articles.title: Why David Krumholtz Was Absent From ’10 Things I Hate About You’ Reunion on ‘DWTS’
articles.author: Carly Thomas

paras.en: David Krumholtz is sharing why he missed the 10 Things I Hate About You reunion during Julia Stiles‘ tribute to Heath Ledger on Dancing With the Stars Tuesday night.
In a video posted on Instagram Wednesday, the actor explained that he’s currently in the Catskill Mountains in upstate New York filming a movie.

“I could not be in L.A. for Dancing With the Stars last night. I would have loved loved loved to have been there,” he said. “Everyone looked so amazing. Julia’s tribute to my dear friend, who I miss every single day, was amazing and stunning, and I’m so proud of her.”

“I thought the cast looked amazing. They all look so young still,” Krumholtz added before taking off his hat to show his newly bald head. He quipped that “it would have been weird” to join his former co-stars in the ballroom after shaving “what’s left of my hair” because it would have become “internet fodder.”
“I didn’t want that, but that’s not why I wasn’t there. I would have dealt with it. Anyway, love them all, love you all,” he concluded.

During the latest DWTS episode, Stiles and her pro partner Ezra Sosa dedicated their dance to Ledger, who starred opposite Stiles in the beloved 1999 rom-com. He died in 2008 at the age of 28 from an accidental overdose.

The pair danced to “Can’t Take My Eyes Off You” by Frankie Valli, which was the song Ledger’s Patrick Verona serenaded Stiles’ Kat Stratford with during her soccer practice at the high school stadium. In the scene, he runs and dances across the stands as the marching band plays to try and win her over after Joey Donner (Andrew Keegan) pays him to take Kat out.

Following Stiles and Sosa’s emotional dance, which featured some of Ledger’s iconic moves, the poem her character reads in the film about Patrick starts playing in the ballroom. After the actress lays a flower on the ground in honor of Ledger, she is joined by her fellow 10 Things I Hate About You co-stars, including Keegan, Joseph Gordon-Levitt (Cameron James), Larisa Oleynik (Bianca Stratford), Gabrielle Union (Chastity) and Susan May Pratt (Mandella).

10 Things I Hate About You, directed by Gil Junger, follows teen Joey who wants to date Bianca, but she can’t date until her antisocial older sister, Kat, has a boyfriend, per her strict father’s rules. That’s when Joey pays a mysterious boy, Patrick, to ask Kat out. In the film, Krumholtz played Michael Eckman, a friend of new student Cameron who also has a crush on Bianca.

articles.title: China's stock market sinks into bear territory as CSI 300 extends 10-week rout

paras.en: China's benchmark CSI 300 index on Thursday entered bear-market territory, falling 20% from its June peak, as a prolonged sell-off in its equities deepens.

The index, which tracks 300 of the largest stocks listed in Shanghai and Shenzhen, has declined for 10 consecutive weeks and is down 2.6% so far this week, underscoring sustained pressure on Chinese equities, data from LSEG showed. The index was more than 1% lower Thursday.

Jordan Cvetanovski, chairman and CIO at Pella Funds, said China's equity market continues to face structural challenges, particularly as the world's second-largest economy grapples with the fallout from years of excess capacity and overinvestment.

"I think China is really struggling with reining in the problems that they've had in the past from the overbuild of capacity and other things," Cvetanovski told CNBC, pointing to challenges facing companies even in globally competitive industries such as batteries — a sector where he still sees select opportunities in China.

Chinese firms have been suffering from declining profit growth amid intense competition that has eroded margins and even invited the government to step in. In September, the country posted it's weakest growth in industrial profits this year.

The world's second-largest economy also posted its slowest growth in over three years in the second quarter, pressured by a multiyear slowdown in the property sector and extended weakness in consumer demand.

Shaun Rein, managing director at China Market Research Group, expects further selling pressure as geopolitical uncertainty, concerns over an artificial intelligence bubble and deteriorating consumer confidence weigh on investor sentiment.
China's large base of retail investors could also exacerbate market volatility, Rein said, as individual investors are prone to exiting the market faster during periods of uncertainty.

Unlike major markets such as the New York Stock Exchange, where retail investors account for about 20%-25% of trade volumes, China's retail investors drive 90% of daily trading, according to data provided by HSBC.

"For Chinese, it's about wealth preservation," Rein said, noting that investors are increasingly favoring safer assets such as time deposits amid a weakening property market and sluggish labor conditions.
While Rein expects increased pressure on markets, he said the sell-off has been excessive, pointing to resilient exports and signs of a recovery in property prices in China's largest cities.
"It's a crisis of confidence right now not a crisis in the economy," he said, predicting a strong rebound in Chinese equities in 2027.

Daniel Gerard, senior multi-asset strategist at State Street Markets, also struck a more optimistic tone, saying that China's growing capabilities in artificial intelligence could eventually draw global investors back into its equity market, even before corporate earnings recover.

articles.title: U.S. pulls diplomats from Saudi Arabia as it reportedly readies Iran strikes after midterms

paras.en: The U.S. ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia as Houthi attacks on the kingdom escalate.

The move comes as the U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, according to The New York Times, citing unnamed U.S. officials.
Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.
The developments point to a possible widening of the nearly eight-month war, while U.S. and Iranian negotiators continue talks on Tehran's nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz.

State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets. Meanwhile, Reuters reported Washington also plans to withdraw family members from other missions in the region.

A strike Wednesday on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam killed at least one person and injured eight. Two people died in a drone attack on Saudi Aramco's Shaybah oil field, the Saudi Press Agency reported, adding that operations were not affected.

In recent days, the U.S. and Israeli militaries have stepped up military exercises, including flying planes over Iraq to practice strike maneuvers, according to The New York Times. The Times also reported that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth met Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during an unannounced visit to Israel this week to discuss potential new strikes.

The renewed military strikes would likely target Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities, and missile and drone arsenal, according to The Times, noting that President Donald Trump has yet to approve the fresh strikes and has repeatedly vetoed plans for a return to major combat this year.
Iranian officials have vowed to widen their attacks to target data centers and undersea internet cables, while refusing concessions on their nuclear program.
Despite the persistent shipping disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, Middle East oil flows through the vital strait have recovered to near pre‑war levels according to Kpler.
As Brent crude topped $110 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate gained 1% to $98.12, recovering appetite for crude from China could drive oil prices higher, according to the commodity research firm.

"China's crude import demand is expected to continue recovering, driven by rising refinery throughput and rapidly declining crude inventories," said Muyu Xu, senior crude oil analyst at Kpler. The war has cut China's oil stockpiles, with the fastest drawndown on record at 1.6 million barrels a day in September, Xu estimated.

China still holds 1.1 billion barrels in reserves, about 80 days of refinery needs, Xu said. She added that with virtually all Iranian cargoes outside the U.S. blockade discharged, substantial new crude arrivals in China appear unlikely.

Chinese state-owned refiners are likely to have a stronger appetite and greater urgency to secure prompt Middle Eastern barrels as they face higher throughput and inventory-replenishment needs. Independent refiners are also seeking alternatives to Iranian crude, a shift that could limit further downside in the Dubai structure, Xu said.

articles.title: Oil prices jump on Middle East worries as U.S., Israel reportedly weigh fresh Iran strikes

paras.en: Oil prices climbed Thursday on worries over a possible escalation in the Middle East conflict as the U.S. reportedly plans to resume strikes against Iran.
Brent crude futures rose 1.71% to $110.67 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude gained 1.42% to $98.53.

The U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections, The New York Times reported, citing unnamed U.S. officials. Planning for a "short but intensive" operation is progressing, The Times said.
The U.S. has also ordered non-emergency government employees and their families to leave Saudi Arabia.

State Department spokesman Tommy Pigott in a post on X said the order applies only to Saudi Arabia, citing increasing attacks by Iran-aligned Houthis on civilian targets, after reports said that the U.S. had directed some staff in the wider Gulf region to leave.

The economic fallout from elevated oil prices, however, may be less severe than in previous decades, as consumers have become less vulnerable to energy shocks, according to David Wagner, head of equity and portfolio manager at Aptus Capital Advisors.
"$100 oil today is very different than $100 oil, you know, 20, 30 years ago," Wagner said, noting that crude prices remain well below their inflation-adjusted historical highs.

He pointed to U.S. government data showing that gasoline accounted for roughly 5% of the average American's disposable income a decade ago, compared with about half that today, suggesting households may be better positioned to withstand elevated energy costs.
"I think we can hold that umbrella over our head ... from the rainstorm of oil," he said.
— CNBC's Anniek Bao contributed to this report.

articles.title: Report pinpoints future exploration sites on the moon

paras.en: The biggest “land rush” of the 21st century is underway—but not on Earth.

Together with multiple international partners, the U.S. and China are racing each other to build crewed outposts around the moon’s south pole, a region rich with water ice and other resources that could be used to kick-start an otherworldly economy and strengthen humanity’s expansion deeper into space. NASA’s Artemis IV mission seeks to send astronauts to the lunar south pole in 2028, and China is targeting human landings there by 2030.

But the clamor to capitalize on that prized patch of lunar real estate shouldn’t overlook other areas on the moon that could be even more valuable for science, according to an authoritative new report. Convened by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, a blue-ribbon panel of experts contends that human sorties to nonpolar regions of the moon hold great promise for resolving long-standing mysteries about Earth’s nearest celestial neighbor, the solar system and the universe at large.

Better yet, the report offers a short list of destinations to prioritize.

The NASA-sponsored report comes from the National Academy of Sciences (NAS) Committee on Key Nonpolar Destinations across the Moon, and it flags four places to send future human missions: Bhabha Crater, Mons Hadley, the Orientale Basin and the Aristarchus Plateau.

“Returning to the moon will be a great achievement for humanity—and setting foot where we never have before will be a major moment for science,” says James Day, co-chair of the committee and a professor at the University of California, San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography.

Visiting these four sites would add immense scientific value to whatever will be learned from any sequence of U.S. and Chinese crewed missions to the lunar south pole, adds committee co-chair Daniel Dumbacher, a professor of engineering practice in the School of Aeronautics and Astronautics at Purdue University.
Dumbacher and Day both discussed their findings in-depth during a webinar shortly after the report’s release.

Bhabha Crater, the report notes, is on the lunar farside and would give astronaut expeditions the ability to access material from the moon’s oldest known preserved impact basin and to deploy ultrasensitive radio and optical astronomy experiments shielded from Earth’s noisy emissions.

The Mons Hadley region, part of which was previously explored by Apollo 15 moonwalkers, is a prime location for a space weather observatory. This site, the report says, could also host experiments to assess how piled-up regolith—impact-pulverized rocks that make up the lunar “soil”—could shield against radiation hazards.

The moon’s Orientale Basin is one of the largest and best-preserved multiringed impact crater in the solar system; going there would give unprecedented looks into the deep structure and origin of our natural satellite. Mission crews, the report adds, should return samples from the basin to Earth to reveal exactly how the basin was formed; while they’re there, they could also deploy a gravitational-wave observatory.

Lastly, the moon’s Aristarchus Plateau is a geologically rich volcanic landscape. Collecting samples there would help researchers understand volcanic processes that have shaped the moon and identify potentially important resources that could support future exploration.

The NAS panel also notes that the moon’s accessibility and sterility make it “an excellent testbed” for refining “planetary protection” procedures—that is, for finding ways to avoid Earth life contaminating other potentially habitable places in the solar system (and ensuring any alien biology doesn’t catastrophically contaminate Earth). Crewed dry runs at lunar test beds could help establish the rules of the road before sending humans to more biologically sensitive environments.

“Practicing planetary protection protocols on the moon will lead to greater confidence in the successful execution of these on other planetary bodies, such as Mars, where life may exist or may once have existed and the stakes are significantly higher,” the report states.

Adding a whole swath of extra proposed crewed lunar landing sites in addition to already planned human forays to the moon’s south pole may seem like overkill, says committee member Clive Neal, a professor of civil and environmental engineering and Earth Sciences at the University of Notre Dame. But the exercise is meant “to be enabling for Artemis and not a distraction.”

“There are four examples given for different missions, but it comes back and feeds into [NASA’s] developing moon base,” he says. One overlooked concept that the report seeks to highlight, Neal adds, is “the idea of a ‘distributed’ moon base”—a network of interlinked sites that can be more than the sum of their parts, providing far more value overall than any solitary outpost.

That’s because the moon probably has much more to offer than just the resources at its shadowy south pole—and figuring out the specifics is a long-term project with far-reaching implications. “There’s both science that enables exploration as well as exploration-driven science that enables a long-term human presence on the moon,” Neal says. “Achieving a permanent human presence on the moon is akin to now having a permanent human presence in low-Earth orbit,” he adds, and the lessons learned will feed forward for future crewed voyages to Mars.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: A “History Book” for the Entire Universe

Jack Burns, a professor emeritus of astrophysics at the University of Colorado Boulder, is delighted by the report’s recommendations. He briefed the specially convened panel regarding a proposed array of low-frequency radio telescopes on the lunar farside.

Called FarView, this facility makes use of the moon’s radio-quiet environment to open the last unexplored electromagnetic window for astrophysics, delivering breakthrough science across astronomy, astrophysics, cosmology, heliophysics and planetary science, he tells Scientific American.

“Astronauts could play a crucial role in the early stages of that array, helping in site surveys, as well as setting up power stations and communications and the basic electronics to get started,” Burns says. The primary science driver for FarView, he adds, is the exploration of the cosmic dark ages, a mysterious era shortly after the big bang and before the formation of the first stars.
As for astronauts conducting such duties versus robots, “the modern way of looking at it is not either; it’s both,” Burns observes.

The NAS report underscores the need to explore the whole moon, not just its south pole, he adds. “The moon is our history book. With Apollo, we just thumbed through the first few pages. But there’s much more to delve into, as the moon is a unique learning tool, not only to understand that body but also to help unwrap the history of our Earth.”

Erica Jawin, a research scientist at the Planetary Science Institute, who was not part of the NAS panel, agrees. Answering questions such as why the moon’s nearside looks so different from its farside, when the giant lunar impact basins formed, and how much water and other “volatile” materials may lurk in the lunar interior would help reveal otherwise-hidden chapters of our planet’s and our solar system’s deepest history.

“These questions, among many others, can be addressed by exploring nonpolar locations,” Jawin says. “The scientific community has repeatedly discussed locations of high scientific value for surface exploration.” The Aristarchus Plateau has been of particular interest.

“The Aristarchus Plateau has been consistently recognized for its scientific value in the form of diverse volcanism and the young, bright Aristarchus Crater, as well as its exploration potential for everything from resource prospecting for water to manufacturing building materials using the thick pyroclastic deposit,” Jawin says.

A robust and successful lunar exploration program, Jawin continues, should leverage the unique role humans can play in conjunction with robotic assets. In particular, it is critical to understand specific locations where scientific exploration would benefit from having a human-crewed component, she said.

“Humans have unique skills for exploration and observation that differ from robotic surface or orbital assets. Particularly, humans excel in visual analyses such as assessing geologic setting and diversity across a landing site, as well as in complex decision-making and confronting unexpected obstacles,” Jawin notes.

With proper investment into scientific and technological capabilities, Jawin concludes, “the coming years could be a renaissance for human exploration of the moon, allowing us to answer scientific questions that have persisted for decades.”

articles.title: Super Typhoon Champi sets the record for strongest storm of 2026

paras.en: A cyclone in the Philippine Sea reached wind speeds of about 185 miles per hour (around 290 kilometers per hour) on Tuesday afternoon EST. Those wind speeds are the strongest of any storm this year, forecasters say.

As of Wednesday morning EST, Super Typhoon Champi had winds of 175 miles per hour; it is expected to weaken in the next day or so, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The storm is currently about 430 nautical miles south of Kadena Air Base in Japan and is heading northwest, according to the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.

You’re more likely to see strong storms in the western Pacific than anywhere else on the planet. But the typhoon underscores how tumultuous Pacific storm activity has been in comparison with activity in the Atlantic. In the North Atlantic, 2026’s strongest storm so far was Hurricane Isaias, which had maximum winds of about 120 mph (193 kph), according to Colorado State University’s (CSU’s) cyclone database. By contrast, in the northeastern Pacific, September’s Hurricane Polo hit wind speeds of about 178 mph (286 kph), while in the northwestern Pacific, April’s Typhoon Sinlaku and July’s Typhoon Bavi also reached around the same strength. Champi is the 25th northwestern Pacific storm this year, according to CSU’s tracker.

To be considered a typhoon or a hurricane, a cyclone must achieve wind speeds of at least 74 mph (119 kph). The designation of hurricane or typhoon depends on where the cyclone occurs. In the Northern Hemisphere, Pacific cyclones that occur west of the international date line are considered typhoons, while those occurring east of that border are categorized as hurricanes.

It’s been a historic year for cyclones. As Scientific American previously reported, the Atlantic has been unusually quiet: Hurricane Isaias was the first storm of its kind for the season, setting a record for the latest-forming first Atlantic hurricane since reliable record-keeping began. Meanwhile the Hawaiian Islands in the Pacific Ocean have seen an unusually high number of hurricanes this season.

Those trends are driven in part by El Niño, a climate pattern that influences weather across the globe. During El Niño years, hurricanes activity tends to slow in the Atlantic and pick up in parts of the Pacific.

articles.title: National Science Foundation leader Brian Stone to retire with no clear replacement in sight

paras.en: The interim head of the National Science Foundation (NSF), Brian Stone, is set to retire as soon as the end of this year, according to reports. There is no clear plan for a successor to steer the agency because President Donald Trump’s nominee to lead the NSF, James O'Neill, has yet to have a confirmation hearing in the Senate.

Stone, who has led the agency since the spring of last year, will resign effective December 31, according to a memo that was sent to NSF staff on Tuesday and was obtained by journalist Dan Garisto. In the note, Stone reportedly wrote that he would be “working closely with the White House to identify who will perform the duties of the NSF Director as of January 1, 2027, should Mr. O’Neill’s nomination still be pending at that time.”
In a statement to Scientific American, NSF spokesperson Mike England appeared to confirm Stone’s upcoming retirement but did not confirm whether he would be leaving at the end of 2026.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

Stone had “served the U.S. National Science Foundation and the American people with distinction for 26 years, including over the past 18 months while performing the duties of NSF Director,” England said in the statement. “His leadership has been instrumental in advancing NSF's mission, and we thank him for his decades of dedicated public service. Brian will continue to perform the duties of the Director until his retirement and NSF will announce any future leadership updates as they are available.”

paras.en: The reported memo also indicated that acting NSF chief of staff Rebecca Keiser will depart as well. England did not confirm or deny this reporting.

Stone has led the NSF on an interim basis since April 2025, after the resignation of the agency’s previous director, Sethuraman Panchanathan, who was appointed during the first Trump presidency in 2019. Panchanathan’s departure came amid Elon Musk’s U.S. DOGE Service cuts, which saw mass staff firings, resignations and axes to grant funding. A staff member of the NSF for more than 25 years, Stone had previously spent 10 years as the agency’s chief of staff.

Stone’s imminent departure comes at a moment of turbulence at the top of the NSF. This past April the Trump administration fired all 22 members of the agency’s science advisory board—these positions are appointed by the president and serve staggered six-year terms. The advisers play a critical role in determining how the NSF disperses the roughly $9 billion in funding it doles out annually. The firings were widely criticized by the scientific community, with thousands of researchers signing an open letter that said it constituted an “alarming attack” on U.S. science. No new board members have since been named .

articles.title: Japan’s sample return mission to Phobos may also collect some Mars dust
articles.author: Meghan Bartels

paras.en: For decades, scientists have dreamed of getting Martian rocks into Earth’s laboratories — a Herculean feat that would revolutionize our knowledge of the Red Planet. An audacious mission from the Japanese space agency might offer the next best thing: rocks from Mars’ larger moon, Phobos.

That’s the task confronting the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft. The mission, which launched October 19, aims to crack the long-standing mystery of how Mars got its two odd moons by delivering a sample of Phobos to Earth in 2031. These rocks are no substitute for true Martian material — but given that NASA’s plans to fetch the Perseverance rover’s prized samples are in limbo, scientists are eager for even an indirect glimpse of Mars.

“It’s a chance to get a totally different sample and view of Martian materials,” says planetary scientist Briony Horgan of Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., who is not involved in the MMX mission. “It’ll be a great contribution to our sample collection back here on Earth.”
If it’s successful, MMX will be the first mission to reach Phobos. Three previous spacecraft from Russia failed.

The MMX itinerary is action-packed: The spacecraft will spend about one year cruising out to Mars, then slip into orbit around Mars alongside Phobos for about three years. During its stay, the spacecraft will deploy a small rover named Idefix to scout the moon for good sampling sites. The main spacecraft will then make two landings to grab 10 grams of sample, about the weight of four U.S. pennies. It will use two different devices to snag the sample: One will drill two centimeters down into the rock, while the other will blow pressurized gas at the surface to collect loose material.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Once loaded up, MMX will zip past the smaller moon Deimos before making the one-year trek home to drop its cargo in Australia’s outback, just as Japan’s two previous asteroid sample-return missions have done. After the Japanese space agency JAXA sorts and catalogs the samples, it will share portions of them with other institutions.

Such a small handful of rock may not sound impressive, but it’s enough to thrill researchers. “A few grams of sample are going to be a real bonanza for scientists,” says planetary scientist Michael Zolensky of NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, where 15 percent of the sample will eventually end up.

MMX is designed to reveal the enigmatic origins of Phobos and Deimos — the only moons in the inner solar system besides our own. “The Martian moons are so different from [the] terrestrial moon: They are two, very small [and] very dark,” says planetary scientist Tomoki Nakamura of Tohoku University in Sendai, Japan.

The strange objects look like rocks that wandered in from the outer asteroid belt and got trapped around Mars. But their tidy circular orbits suggest they coalesced after a massive collision tore material off the Red Planet. Or perhaps they came about some other way that scientists simply haven’t imagined, says planetary scientist Kiyoshi Kuramoto of Hokkaido University in Sapporo, Japan. “The natural world often reveals aspects that exceed our expectations,” he says.

Studying the features and composition of Phobos’ surface could solve the mystery. But although MMX carries sophisticated instruments to explore Phobos, those observations may not suffice. Hence bringing rock back to Earth’s labs, where scientists can enlist equipment far too large or delicate to ever send to space.

Although sample analysis will focus on understanding Phobos, researchers will also be able to use the rocks to fine-tune our understanding of Mars. For example, pinpointing the material’s age will allow scientists to calibrate the chronology of cosmic collisions in the neighborhood of Mars. Currently, scientists estimate ages on Mars based on a timeline based on our moon, which may not apply at the Red Planet.

Scientists even have reason to hope that stray grains from Mars will be hidden amid the MMX treasure. This material could be ancient relics of the two bodies mixing during a moon-forming process, potentially including grains that hail from deeper in the Martian crust than scientists have seen so far in rare meteorites the cosmos has delivered us. No matter how Phobos formed, the material could also include fresher debris flung off the Red Planet by cosmic collisions.

The biggest challenge may be positively identifying which grains came from Mars. Such lucky samples would lack valuable geologic context and be far from pristine. “They’re material that’s been blasted off Mars from some unknown location, micron-sized things, sitting on the airless body Phobos, getting irradiated by space,” says planetary scientist Nancy Chabot of the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory in Laurel, Md. Nonetheless, scientists are prepared to get creative and use the latest technology to tease out every secret they can manage in any sample they can snag.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: MMX offers a very different type of sample return than what NASA has initiated with the Perseverance rover, which has spent years squirreling away fresh material drilled from the most interesting outcrops it can find. That’s all in hopes of a future mission ferrying the rock to Earth for scientists to hunt for signs of ancient microbes. But the U.S. Congress has axed funding for that successor due to spiraling costs and concerns about feasibility — particularly of accomplishing the first ever launch from Mars.

paras.en: Even if MMX can’t give scientists the satisfaction of an ultimate Mars sample return, there’s still plenty to learn, says planetary scientist Vicky Hamilton of the Southwest Research Institute in Boulder, Colo., who is not involved in the mission. “It’s always a happy day when we’re getting a sample from another object in space and bringing it back to Earth to study,” she says.

articles.title: These tiny snakes cartwheel to escape danger
articles.author: Maria Temming

paras.en: Cartwheeling seems like it should require both arms and legs. But some itty-bitty snakes in Southeast Asia manage it without either.

Scientists first shared snapshots of a dwarf reed snake (Pseudorabdion longiceps) cartwheeling away from danger in 2023. Now, videos of three Pseudorabdion species hightailing it down a racetrack in the lab have offered a closer look at this rare and strangely acrobatic behavior.

Each snake starts with its body curled into a C shape, head lifted off the ground and facing the way it’s going. It then whips its tail out behind it, briefly becoming airborne. The snake flips its tail forward and down past its head. When the snake’s tail hits the ground in front of it, another roll begins, researchers report October 19 in Current Biology.

“What a cool snake behavior,” says Jessica Tingle, a biologist at Brown University in Providence, R.I., not involved in the work. “I find it especially amazing that an elongate animal like a snake can manage to roll, especially given that they do it in such an explosive way, which probably asks a lot of their muscles and bones.”

Yosuke Kojima was equally surprised when a colleague in Sarawak, Malaysia recounted witnessing this “very weird” behavior in 2019. So the researchers collected snakes from Malaysia’s Kubah National Park. They scooped up 11 P. saravacense, one P. collaris, one P. longiceps, plus six Calamaria reed snakes for comparison.

Finding the snakes was no easy task. They were only about 11 to 28 centimeters long. “They always hide under the leaves,” says Kojima, an ecologist at Toho University in Chiba, Japan. But were any of the snakes able to cartwheel away from the researchers? “No,” Kojima laughs. “We are quicker than them.”

The team set up a 2.2-meter-long racetrack and placed the snakes one at a time at one end. A gentle tap coaxed the snakes to move and cameras above and beside the track recorded the action. None of the Calamaria snakes cartwheeled, but all of the Pseudorabdion snakes did. At full tilt, they tumbled at 1.7 to 3.7 meters per second — about six to 13 kilometers per hour.
Through it all, the snakes held their heads fairly steady — reminiscent of how flying snakes hold their heads stable while launching into the air, the researchers say.

A cartwheeling snake first rolls its body along the ground to whip its tail out behind its head. Then, it swings its tail up and over its head. Finally, it brings its tail down on either the left or right side of its head. Once it the tail hits the ground, the snake is ready for another roll. In the cartwheel seen on top, the snake brings its tail down on the left side of its head, angling its whitish belly toward the viewer. In the cartwheel on the bottom, the snake’s tail lands on the right side of its head, showing its darker back to the viewer.

paras.en: “I am very curious how such a strange and possibly demanding movement evolved … whether dwarf reed snakes have something special in their anatomy, physiology or neural control that lets them do it when their close relatives apparently can’t or don’t,” Tingle says. “Are their brains different in some way to let them coordinate a fast and unusual movement? Or do all snakes have the basic equipment, and they just don’t use it?”
Those may be open mysteries. But catching snakes cartwheeling on camera does tie up one loose end for Tingle.

“Some writers in the 1800s talked about ‘hoop snakes’ and described their motion as rolling, but that seemed pretty fantastical to me, and I chalked it up to overly inventive imaginations,” Tingle says. Those 19th century authors may or may not have been describing the exact behavior Kojima’s team recorded. “Either way, it’s neat to find out a real animal does something reminiscent of a fantastical old story.”

articles.title: What can minerals tell us about Earth’s past? This geologist is finding out
articles.author: Anna Mattson

paras.en: This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback?

The minute Gabriela Farfan stepped into a small natural history museum in Madison, Wis., where she grew up, she knew she wanted to work with minerals. Farfan remembers seeing all different shapes and colors and being enthralled. “From that point forward, I knew I wanted to become a geologist someday,” she says.

Farfan is now living her teenage dream as the curator of gems and minerals at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C. Her specialty is biomineralization — how organisms build skeletons, corals, pearls and shells. Farfan hopes to answer questions about how they form and what stories they tell by studying crystal structures and the chemistry of minerals.

These days, she investigates signals trapped within minerals. Corals, for example, build layers of calcium carbonate mineral over time, trapping chemical signatures from the ocean. The data tell all kinds of stories — about stress, disease outbreaks and changes to ocean temperature and sea level. Farfan unlocks those tales using X-ray and Raman spectroscopies, bouncing beams off samples to see what they can tell us.

She hopes museum visitors will remember that the sparkly gemstones, the ones that first enamored her, are just as natural as the plants and bones in other exhibits. “Minerals are actual natural history objects,” Farfan says. “Those are actually formed by Mother Nature and it’s spectacular.”

articles.title: One-Quarter of Data Centers Are Located in Water-Stressed Areas, Study Shows
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: Data centers need water to stay cool and functional, and lots of it: The larger facilities can consume as much water a day as a town of 50,000 people, and because much of the cooling involves evaporation, freshwater is often preferred.

That raises serious questions about the environmental impact of the cloud compute we use to run AI queries, host photos and videos, stream music, and all the rest. Researchers are trying to get a handle on what the impacts on water usage actually are.

In a new study published in Environmental Science & Technology, researchers led by a team from the Carnegie Institution for Science in the US mapped the location of the 9,347 currently identified data centers worldwide.

When the local water conditions of all these sites were analyzed, the team found that around 25 percent of data centers are in areas where there's a water gap during at least one month of the year – that's when water demand outstrips supply.

Based on climate models and 3 °C (5.4 °F) of average global temperature rise from 1900 levels, the number of water-stressed data center locations would rise to 33 percent within as little as 10 years, the researchers found.

"These facilities are not landing in empty landscapes," says environmental scientist Lorenzo Rosa, from the Carnegie Institution for Science. "They are landing on top of the water supply of cities and farms."

While electricity can be spread across long distances through a power grid, the same can't be said for water. It typically needs to be sourced locally, which means the local conditions at sites chosen for data centers really do matter.
Water typically gets pulled from lakes, rivers, and aquifers – which can all vary seasonally in terms of the water they supply.

"The energy footprint of data centers has been quantified in detail because electricity is metered and reported," says Rosa. "Water scarcity is measured locally, inconsistently, and often not at all."
"So, we built the map because it did not exist."

The map showed that 41 percent of global data centers are competing directly with cities and municipalities for their water, while for another 28 percent of sites the primary water use is for agriculture.
For 523 facilities – that's a little over 5 percent of the total – there are already water gaps for at least 9 months of the year.

There were differences in terms of climate change impact too. Most data centers pushed beyond the water gap threshold by temperature rises would be in the US, the modeling showed, while in countries such as the UK and Germany there wouldn't be much change.
"Data centers typically have the financial capacity and institutional priority to secure water supplies whenever water is available," write the researchers in their published paper.
"As a result, the primary risk may not be to data center operations themselves but to other water users within the same basins."

The researchers note that information on data center water usage remains limited – the giant tech companies involved are reticent to share the exact level of demand these facilities are putting on our natural resources.
More accountable reporting would definitely help, which might require intervention from regulators and governments.

There is some positivity from the researchers at the end of their paper, though, pointing to efforts to use wastewater and treated seawater in place of freshwater, as well as improvements in data center heat management. What's clear is that changes are needed before the data center water drain gets worse.

"The extent to which water-stress exposure translates into operational impacts for data centers themselves or into measurable consequences for other water users remains an open question to address," write the researchers.
"Ensuring data center long-term viability will require siting and governance choices that account for local hydrological limits."
The research has been published in Environmental Science & Technology.

articles.title: 'Low-Oxygen' Drug Combination Reverses Parkinson's Symptoms in Mice
articles.author: Esra Öz

paras.en: Our brains depend on a steady oxygen supply, and problems can arise when cells cannot properly use the oxygen reaching them.
Scientists investigating what happens when that balance breaks down have tested an unexpected approach in mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms: reducing oxygen delivery to their tissues.
Mice given an experimental drug combination became quicker at descending a pole and could hold onto a cage lid for longer. Treatment began after their movement problems had already appeared.
The researchers call their approach "hypoxia in a pill" because it recreates some effects of breathing low-oxygen air.
Parkinson's damages brain cells that produce dopamine, a chemical that helps regulate movement. The disease also involves the buildup of a protein called alpha-synuclein.
Damage associated with this protein can disrupt the tiny energy-producing structures inside cells, called mitochondria. These structures use oxygen to help generate energy.

"Our current working hypothesis is that when there is mitochondrial dysfunction, oxygen is not being consumed properly, and this leads to an oxygen mismatch, i.e., oxygen delivery is greater than oxygen utilization," Harvard Medical School physician-scientist Vamsi K. Mootha told ScienceAlert.
By reducing oxygen delivery, the team aims to limit that mismatch and the damage that comes with it.

In a 2025 study, the researchers showed that mice with Parkinson's-like symptoms benefited from continuously breathing air with 11 percent oxygen. Ordinary air contains about 21 percent. In the new study, they tested whether drugs could achieve similar effects.

Hong Wang and colleagues used two compounds that complement each other. The first, GBT601, makes the blood release less of its oxygen into tissues. Because the body can compensate by producing more oxygen-carrying red blood cells, the second compound, PT2399, limits that response.

For the experiment, the scientists injected alpha-synuclein fibrils into the mice's brains to trigger protein buildup and movement difficulties. Six weeks later, once movement problems had developed, they began giving the drugs orally each day.

Over the following six weeks, treated animals improved in the pole and cage-hang tests, while mice given only the injection of liquid without the protein solution kept getting worse. The combination also reduced excess brain oxygen and lowered a marker of fat damage in brain tissue, but did not improve an anxiety-like behavior measure.
Mootha said improvements with either inhaled low oxygen or the drug approach can begin as early as one to two weeks after treatment starts.

Better movement does not show that nerve cells have been restored. Mootha explained that in the 2025 experiment, mice already had movement problems when delayed treatment began, but no nerve cell loss had been detected yet. The mice regained movement abilities and avoided subsequent nerve cell loss even though the buildup of alpha-synuclein remained unchanged.
The new study did not report dopamine neuron counts in the main paper, so it does not establish whether the combination protects those cells.

The team also tried the combination in two other disease models. In mice modeling Leigh syndrome, a rare disorder affecting cellular energy production, the combination extended median lifespan from 62 to 158 days. In a model of Friedreich's ataxia, which affects movement and coordination, it stopped further deterioration without reversing existing difficulties.
After six weeks of treatment in control mice, the researchers found no increase in a heart measurement linked to pulmonary hypertension, a risk of prolonged low oxygen.
"Hypoxia can be dangerous, so an important challenge is being able to achieve hypoxia therapy that is safe and effective," Mootha cautioned.
"All of our work to date is pre-clinical, in mouse models, and much more work is required before moving this concept into humans."
The research has been published in PNAS.

articles.title: New Fossil Confirms a Human Ancestor Appeared 200,000 Years Earlier Than Expected
articles.author: David Nield

paras.en: The fossil record shows that our Homo erectus ancestors were the first hominins to show signs of adapting to life on the ground, with longer legs and shorter arms emerging (the name translates to 'upright human').

It's therefore important that anthropologists can date the species correctly – and a new fossil analysis from an international team of researchers, published in the Annals of Human Biology, pushes back the emergence of these proto-people by about 200,000 years.

Imagine archaeologists of the distant future digging up the first iPhone and finding it wasn't invented in 2007, as previously assumed, but appeared in the time of Neanderthals and woolly mammoths. That's the sort of timescale we're talking about.

The discovery comes from the Drimolen Main Quarry near Johannesburg in South Africa, a hugely significant site for early humans known as the 'Cradle of Humankind'. What's more, the study includes additional findings for a more distant ancient human relative.

"This paper publishes a new adult fossil attributed to Homo erectus, DNH 127, providing further confirmation that this species first appeared in southern Africa 2 million years ago," says archaeologist Jesse Martin, from La Trobe University in Australia.
The adjusted timeline isn't completely new, because a skull fragment designated as DNH 134 had already been dated to the same period.
However, DNH 134 belonged to a young child, making comparisons with adults tricky.

A total of 18 fossils were analyzed in this latest research, with the physical characteristics of the bones used to identify each species, and geological techniques, including radioactive dating, used to determine the age of the fossils.

Besides the single DNH 127 fossil for H. erectus, the team also linked 14 fossils to another hominin, Paranthropus robustus. This ancient relative is farther from us than H. erectus on the family tree, and had heavy jaws and big teeth for processing food that was hard and tough.
At the same time as H. erectus was evolving larger brains and smaller teeth, the teeth of P. robustus were getting bigger, and their chewing muscles were getting stronger (shown by jaw shapes).
Ultimately, it would be the H. erectus lineage that survived.
"These two human species shared the same landscape and are both preserved in the Drimolen cave," says Martin.
"While we know that Homo erectus and the lineage leading to us was ultimately the successful one, 2 million years ago P. robustus outnumbered Homo erectus at Drimolen by more than 10 to one."

The P. robustus discoveries back up the idea that the species was evolving over time. Other fossils from the same species found in other locations suggested larger, stronger hominins, a sign of the species changing.
Overall, the new P. robustus fossils revealed some characteristics in jaw structure that hadn't been seen before, and several areas of variation.
"The large number of fossils from Drimolen, some of which are published in this paper, allow an unprecedented insight into the micro-evolutionary changes that shaped human ancestors," says Martin.

We already knew ancient human ancestry was complicated, with multiple species overlapping in different places rather than following along one after another. This latest study adds some clarity for two species in the Drimolen region.

It's worth bearing in mind that the fossils here are relatively small fragments, and further investigation will be required to confirm the presence of H. erectus and P. robustus this far back in time. The good news is there are a lot of discovered fossils to study at this site, and most likely more to be dug up.
There may well be more to find here to help understand why the P. robustus evolutionary line eventually died out, and ultimately, H. erectus likely led to modern-day humans.
"During this time period it was our [H. erectus] ancestors that looked like the outside long-odds chance to survive," says Martin.
The research has been published in The Annals of Human Biology.

articles.title: Just 4 minutes a day can dramatically improve strength after 65

paras.en: Just 4 minutes a day can dramatically improve strength after 65

- A new Penn State study suggests that just four minutes of daily strength training can significantly improve mobility and physical function in older adults. After 12 weeks, participants showed meaningful gains in balance, leg strength, and their ability to stand up from a chair, all important factors for maintaining independence and reducing fall risk.

A daily strength training routine lasting just four minutes can significantly improve strength, balance, and mobility in older adults, according to new research led by Penn State College of Medicine. The findings suggest that maintaining physical independence with age may require much less exercise than many people assume.

Published in the journal PLOS One, the study found that adults aged 65 and older experienced meaningful improvements in physical performance after only 12 weeks. These gains are especially important because muscle strength and mobility influence the risk of falling, the ability to live independently, and overall health and longevity.

For older adults, being able to move comfortably and perform everyday activities is essential for maintaining quality of life. Simple tasks such as standing up from a chair, climbing stairs, and walking can become more difficult as strength and balance decline.
According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, unintentional injuries, including those caused by falls, are among the leading causes of death in adults aged 65 and older.

Despite the importance of physical fitness, many older adults believe that meaningful improvements require long, demanding workouts. Christopher Sciamanna, professor of medicine and public health at Penn State College of Medicine and lead author of the study, says the new findings challenge that assumption. Even a brief daily routine can improve important measures of mobility and physical function.

"The human body is designed to improve very quickly," Sciamanna said. "And just a few repetitions of an exercise performed regularly can lead to huge improvements. Exercise is about forward thinking -- think about what you want to be able to do and train for it."
Why Shorter Workouts Could Make Exercise Easier

Strength training, also known as resistance training, involves making muscles work against some form of resistance, such as body weight or elastic bands. Research has shown that it can substantially improve muscle strength within a few months.

However, fewer than one in five older adults meet the recommendation to perform muscle strengthening activities at least twice a week. Common obstacles include discomfort, limited time, and the physical demands of conventional exercise programs.
Another challenge is that planning an effective workout can feel overwhelming, particularly for people who are unfamiliar with exercise.

"Exercise is actually really complicated, because you have to decide how many repetitions, how far, how many sets, how much rest, and how many times per week," said co-author Smita Dandekar, associate professor of pediatrics at Penn State College of Medicine. "It's hard work, so there's huge problems with people wanting to do exercise. If we can make it short, we're part way there."

The researchers had already seen encouraging results from an earlier experiment called FAST (Functional Activity Strength Training)-1. In that smaller study, 24 older adults performed just 30 seconds of push-ups and squats each day. After six months, their ability to perform squats had improved.
Other research has similarly suggested that performing only a few sets of exercises each week can produce strength improvements approaching those achieved with considerably longer workouts.
These findings led Sciamanna and his colleagues to investigate whether an especially brief exercise program could produce measurable improvements in older adults.
Testing a Simple Four-Minute Exercise Routine
For the new study, the Penn State researchers developed a program called FAST-2 to evaluate whether a short daily workout could improve mobility and physical ability in adults older than 65.
The trial included 97 participants whose average age was 74. They were randomly divided into two groups, with one following the exercise program and the other receiving no intervention.

Before the study began, participants reported exercising for an average of only about 18 minutes per week. That was far below the general recommendation of at least 150 minutes of moderate physical activity or 75 minutes of vigorous activity each week, Sciamanna explained.
The FAST-2 routine consisted of four simple movements:
- Push-ups: To strengthen muscles in the upper body.
- Chair stands: Repeatedly standing up from a seated position to work the legs.
- Two-arm rows: Pulling against resistance to strengthen the upper body.
- Stair stepping: Stepping up and down to challenge the legs and support functional mobility.
Each exercise lasted 30 seconds, followed by 30 seconds of rest, bringing the complete routine to four minutes.

Participants received four elastic resistance bands and an adjustable-height stepper, along with written instructions explaining how to perform each movement. The researchers also provided easier variations to accommodate different physical abilities.

For example, participants could perform push-ups against a wall or countertop rather than on the floor. Those who found chair stands challenging could use their hands on their knees for additional support.

As their strength improved, participants were encouraged to make the exercises progressively more difficult. Someone performing modified push-ups might advance to the standard movement, while another participant might increase the height of the stepper.

To evaluate the program, researchers measured how quickly and effectively participants could rise from a chair and how long they could balance on one leg. These assessments were conducted at the beginning, midpoint, and end of the 12-week study.

Such tests are valuable because they reflect movements people rely on throughout the day. Performance on these assessments can also help predict future mobility problems, fall risk, and the potential need for additional care.
Significant Strength and Balance Improvements in Just 12 Weeks
The results showed that the brief exercise program produced significant gains in physical function, even though it involved only 60 seconds of lower body resistance training per session.
Participants demonstrated several measurable improvements:
- 4.2 additional chair stands: An increase in the number of times participants could stand up from a chair within 30 seconds.
- 3.6 more seconds of balance: An improvement in how long participants could remain standing on one leg.
- 2.3 seconds faster: A reduction in the time needed to complete the sit-to-stand assessment.

These changes may seem modest, but they reflect physical abilities that are essential for everyday independence. Stronger legs and better balance can make activities such as getting out of a chair, climbing stairs, and walking easier to perform.
Sciamanna emphasized that these simple physical tests can reveal important information about a person's future health and independence.

"These indicators predict your future ability to go into a nursing home, your future likelihood of falling and of developing difficulty walking," Sciamanna said. "They give you a sense of whether or not you're going to be able to be active in the future."

Although the study measured improvements in physical performance rather than directly testing whether participants experienced fewer falls or avoided nursing home care, the findings suggest that short workouts could help preserve abilities closely tied to independent living.
A Workout Older Adults Can Actually Stick With
Beyond the improvements in strength and mobility, the researchers identified another major advantage of the four-minute routine: participants were able to follow it consistently.
Throughout the study, they completed their exercises on 81% of days.

That level of participation suggests that a short, straightforward workout may be easier to incorporate into daily life than a longer exercise program. It could also help people overcome obstacles such as limited time, discomfort, or difficulty maintaining a regular fitness routine.
For older adults who are largely inactive, even a small amount of consistent resistance training could therefore provide a practical starting point for improving physical function.

The researchers say their results reinforce the idea that exercise sessions do not need to be lengthy to produce meaningful benefits. By focusing on movements that support everyday activities, a few minutes of daily effort may help older adults maintain strength, mobility, and independence.

For Sciamanna, the ultimate purpose of exercise extends beyond simply becoming physically stronger. It is about preserving the ability to participate in life and continue doing the things that matter most.

"Exercise is the key to freedom," he said. "Freedom is the ability to be able to do what you want to do, and I would say that if you can't do what you want to do, you're not free. I approach exercise by thinking of what I want to be able to do in 20 years, and then I train to do that."

Additional Penn State researchers involved in the study included Smita Dandekar of the Department of Pediatrics, Division of Hematology and Oncology at Penn State Health Children's Hospital; Jordan Kurth, Liza S. Rovniak, Noel Ballentine, and Natalia Pierwola-Gawin of the Department of Medicine, Division of General Internal Medicine at Penn State College of Medicine; and Yimeng Shang and Shouhao Zhou of the Department of Public Health Sciences, Division of Biostatistics and Bioinformatics at Penn State College of Medicine.

articles.title: Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells

paras.en: Rejuvenation breakthrough: Scientists reverse 60 years of aging in human cells

- Scientists have turned blood cells from an 80-year-old into neural stem cells with a molecular age of less than 20, effectively reversing more than 60 years of cellular aging in the laboratory. The discovery offers a new way to investigate how cells become younger and could help researchers better understand age-related diseases such as Alzheimer's.

Scientists in Germany have found a way to dramatically reverse the molecular age of human cells, transforming blood cells from an 80-year-old person into stem cells with an age signature of less than 20 years.

Researchers at the University Hospital of Bonn and the University of Bonn achieved this remarkable transformation by reprogramming immature red blood cells into neural stem cells, which can eventually develop into brain cells. During the process, molecular markers associated with aging were effectively reset, making the cells more than 60 years younger at the molecular level.

Unlike earlier approaches, the rejuvenation happened gradually, allowing scientists to follow the changes over an extended period. This slower process could provide important clues about how cellular aging can be reversed and potentially help researchers investigate treatments for diseases associated with aging.
The findings were published in the journal Aging Cell.
How Scientists Turn Blood Cells Into Brain Stem Cells

The human body contains hundreds of specialized cell types, all of which originate from a single fertilized egg and carry essentially the same genetic instructions. As cells develop, however, they take on specific roles. Under normal circumstances, a skin cell cannot transform into a liver cell, and a blood cell cannot become a nerve cell.

Modern laboratory techniques have made it possible to overcome these biological restrictions. Scientists can now reprogram certain mature cells to adopt entirely different identities. For example, skin cells can be converted into cells capable of producing nerve tissue, an approach that could eventually contribute to treatments for neurodegenerative diseases.

The process relies on a combination of proteins called transcription factors, which regulate how genes are activated. By changing which genetic instructions a cell follows, these proteins can redirect its development and give it a new cellular identity.

"Using this method, we have directly converted red blood cell precursors into neural stem cells," explains Prof. Dr. Oliver Brüstle, director of the Institute of Reconstructive Neurobiology at the University Hospital of Bonn.

Earlier experiments by the Bonn team had already demonstrated that nerve cells generated through this approach could successfully connect with existing neurons after being transplanted into the brains of mice.
Scientists Reverse More Than 60 Years of Cellular Aging
The latest investigation focused on an especially intriguing consequence of cellular reprogramming: the dramatic reversal of molecular aging.

"In our current study, however, we focused on a different phenomenon: namely, the observation that cells become significantly rejuvenated during reprogramming," emphasizes Brüstle, who is also a member of the Transdisciplinary Research Area (TRA) Life & Health at the University of Bonn.

To determine how much the cells had rejuvenated, the researchers examined their molecular clocks, particularly biological markers known as epigenetic clocks. These clocks estimate a cell's biological age by analyzing chemical modifications to DNA that tend to accumulate or change as organisms grow older.

Importantly, these modifications do not alter the DNA sequence itself. Instead, they affect how frequently certain genetic instructions are used (epigenetics). Because these patterns change predictably with age, scientists can use them to estimate how old a cell appears at the molecular level.

The results were striking. After reprogramming, cells taken from an 80-year-old individual displayed molecular age signatures corresponding to someone younger than 20. In other words, the process had reversed more than six decades of cellular aging.
"We also know that this epigenetic rejuvenation ensures that the cells actually behave like young cells," says the scientist.
A Slower Rejuvenation Process Reveals New Clues

Scientists have previously observed that reprogramming cells can reset their biological age. However, earlier demonstrations of this effect involved a more complicated process requiring two distinct stages.

First, researchers would convert an existing cell, such as a blood cell, into a pluripotent stem cell. These versatile cells have nearly unlimited developmental "career paths" because they can give rise to many different cell types throughout the body.
The pluripotent stem cell would then be guided into becoming a neural stem cell, which is more specialized and can produce cells found in the nervous system.
This conventional approach produces rejuvenation relatively quickly, making it difficult to examine all the changes taking place.
The Bonn researchers instead bypassed the pluripotent stage entirely.

"In contrast, we converted blood cells directly into neural stem cells -- that is, without first passing through the pluripotent cell stage," said Brüstle. "In our approach, rejuvenation occurred gradually and could be tracked for over 100 days."

The researchers observed a dramatic reduction in molecular age, with the study highlighting rejuvenation of approximately 60 years after 50 days. Because the process continued over a much longer period, scientists could examine the biological changes as they unfolded rather than observing only the final result.
What Cellular Rejuvenation Could Mean for Alzheimer's Research
The ability to watch cells gradually become younger could be particularly valuable for scientists trying to understand the mechanisms that control biological aging.
By studying this extended transformation, researchers can investigate which molecular pathways are involved and test whether particular substances can speed up or slow down the rejuvenation process.

"Rejuvenation that extends over such a long period of time is ideal as an experimental model: Since the epigenetic clocks are slowly reset over several weeks, we can use this model to investigate which factors and active substances accelerate or slow down the rejuvenation process."

The findings could be especially relevant to neuroscience, where aging is closely connected to the development of serious neurological conditions. Although the work does not establish a treatment capable of reversing aging in people, it offers a laboratory model for investigating how cells regain youthful characteristics.
This could eventually help scientists better understand the cellular changes associated with conditions such as Alzheimer's disease.
"After all, age is the most important risk factor for neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer's!"

The research involved teams from the University Hospital of Bonn, the University of Bonn, and RWTH Aachen University. Funding was provided by the EU's Horizon 2020 program, the German Research Foundation (DFG), and the Federal Ministry of Research, Technology, and Space (BMFRT).
